pitch_detail.notes: Follow the Sunrise Mine Trail about half a mile. Just before it crosses the South Fork Stillaguamish, leave it for a faint abandoned path on the river's east side. The path comes and goes and soon vanishes into slide alder and brush, worst around 2,700 ft. Fording the river to dodge the brush is not safe when the water is high.

Keep working up the east side of the valley past a house-sized boulder near 3,000–3,100 ft. One option crosses the river here and climbs a ridge ramp southwest to an upper basin at 4,000 ft, which is brushier. The other follows the river to the broad basin at about 3,700 ft below Del Campo's north face. In spring this ground is piled with hard, lumpy avalanche debris shed off the slabs.

From the 3,700-ft basin turn sharply right up the steep gully directly east, or the slabs on its right. Leave it to the right once that is easy. At a headwall near 4,400 ft either climb straight up or go around through the trees, which is the easier line on snow and on the way down. The gully often holds snow into early summer, with water running down its middle.

Climb the slabs northwest to a notch in Morning Star's southeast ridge at about 5,600 ft. The summit comes into view on this flatter ground. These slabs hold snow well into the season and are the route's main avalanche concern. Close to the notch the snow can be icy under fresh snow, so put crampons on before it steepens.

From the notch drop roughly 100–200 ft through trees into the southeast basin (about 5,400 ft). Traverse right below the cliffs to the first broad gully and climb it to the south ridge about 250 ft below the summit. Filled with snow, the gully runs near 45° and is often icy, so crampons are standard. When the snow is bad, the rocks on its right are an alternative, but they are exposed.

Climb north on or near the south ridge over the last 200–250 ft of steep ground to the 6,020-ft summit. Early in the day the west-facing slope below the top can stay icy, so mix rock, heather and snow to avoid the iced patches. Descend the same way, taking particular care in the gully below.

wa_morning_star_peak_standard.overview: Morning Star Peak (6,020 ft) sits above Headlee Pass and the Sunrise Mine basin between Sperry and Del Campo Peaks, in the Mountain Loop Highway corridor of the Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest (Darrington Ranger District). The standard route leaves the Sunrise Mine Trail about half a mile in, before the South Fork Stillaguamish crossing, and climbs the brushy river valley and snow-covered slabs to a notch in the southeast ridge, then a steep gully to the south ridge and the summit. The South Ridge scramble is rated T5/S4 — a 'rugged, beautiful and challenging true scramble' requiring comfort on steep rock and snow — tougher than the Class 2-3 label alone suggests, especially in early season. Route-finding takes some care, and the snow-covered slabs below the notch are the route's main avalanche concern.

wa_lemah_two_goatshead_spire.descent_text: No descent description for the spire exists. Plan on rappelling what you climb, which on an unrepeated 1982 line means carrying enough cord and slings to build and leave anchors. Below the tower, the retreat is the reverse of the approach: back down through the cirque, down the snow finger, down the class 2-3 step beside the small waterfall, then the flagged climbers' path on the north bank of Lemah Creek back to the PCT, and 7-plus trail miles out via the PCT junction and Pete Lake. Budget for finishing in the dark — parties on the neighbouring standard route routinely do.

wa_nooksack_tower_south_face.descent_text: The first-ascent party downclimbed/rappelled from the summit via the standard north face route on the front (north) side of the tower rather than retracing the South Face, then reversed the glacier approach back to camp.

wa_davis_peak_nc_north_face.descent_text:
The 2005 party's words: 'Stuart doesn't fancy descending to the river any more than I do. So, one way or another; we're going down the other side.' That is the correct call — the northeast face has no easy retreat, and the south side, though long and unpleasant, is walkable.

From the top of the couloir at about 6,700 ft, rappel from pitons onto the SE ridge (or continue up the ridge to the 7,054 ft summit first if the clock allows). Descend the south side following the South Slope and Ridge route in reverse: down the ridge crest, past the 5,720+ ft saddle, over or around Point 5872, and then straight down the sustained trackless forest of the south slope to the highway.

The key is daylight. The 2005 party got the upper 1,500 ft done in the light and credit that with saving them; it let them avoid all the cliff bands and the rappelling-off-trees that comes with getting them wrong. They reached the top of the timber just after dark, found the forest thick but not as bad as feared — no cliffs and not much slide alder on their line — and took four hours from there to the road. The timber is dense enough that they never saw the lights from the dam the whole way down; the only lights they saw were a car's, a few hundred feet above the highway. A bit of compass work is what kept them from ending up back in Stetattle Creek.

You finish at the Gorge Creek bridge, about four highway miles from where you parked in Diablo. Arrange a shuttle car — retrieving the truck cost the 2005 party another half hour on foot at the end of a two-day climb.
wa_davis_peak_nc_north_face.rappels: No fixed anchors and no established rappel line. The rock is compact enough that the 2005 party wrote that 'rap anchors aren't going to be leaping out at you' — retreating from mid-face means leaving pins. On topping out they rappelled from pitons off the top of the couloir onto the SE ridge and then walked the south side down. Carry a pin rack and tat if you want the option of going back down the face.

wa_the_l_h_route_free_variation.beta: Shares its start with The Tiger before splitting into its own line. Quality 5.10 climbing (some sections still lichen-flecked) is interspersed with harder cruxes on immaculate rock; grades are described by the first free ascensionists as "theoretical" given the route has seen very few repeats. The original 1969 aid pitches used roughly 1.5 billion pitons and 1 bolt; the free ascent added 3 protection bolts (with FA-party Jim Langdon's permission) on sections that had been aided via upward-driven knifeblade pitons.
